name: Nora Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for making the time, Nora. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, party or union, and what you say is kept confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage the payroll team at a large parcel delivery company, six payroll officers at the head office. We pay about four thousand drivers and warehouse staff every month, and every one of them notices if their overtime is wrong. My day is checking exceptions, signing off the pay run, and answering emails that start with 'I've been underpaid'.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's exact. Either the numbers balance or they don't, and when they balance on the last Thursday of the month, I go home happy. What wears me down is the night shift timesheets, which come in late and messy, and the drivers who ring me personally because they've got my number from someone.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a flat I bought three years ago, with a small mortgage. I've got about ten months of money saved, because my dad drilled it into me. I don't use those AI chat tools at all. I've got a spreadsheet for everything, and I trust it because I built it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was always going to be a tool, not a takeover. At work I'd say payroll still needs someone who'll be blamed if it's wrong. I don't post online, so I'd just say it over lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still feel a bit watched. Payroll is the kind of routine screen work the card says gets automated, even in the small version. If the timesheet matching gets done by software, that's a third of my team's week gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job exactly as I do now. I'd keep saving, and I'd pay a bit extra off the mortgage, because I hate owing money. If they brought in a tool, I'd learn what I had to and nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, with a small knot in my stomach about the matching software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the payroll project you mentioned already happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, sort of. There's a project called Payroll Simplification, and IT keep asking my team for examples of how we check timesheets. Nobody has said the payroll project is about cutting jobs, but nobody has said it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if your team were cut to five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make sure it was fair, that the one who left had a good reference and a proper payout. I'd be fine, I think. They need someone senior enough to sign off the pay run, and that's me.

say: I'd say AI was always going to be a **tool**, not a takeover.
I'd say payroll needs someone who'll be **blamed if it's wrong**.
think: **Timesheet matching** is a third of my team's week, and software could take it.
The **Payroll Simplification** project makes me feel watched, even in this picture.
do: Keep doing the job **exactly as now**.
Pay a bit **extra off the mortgage** each month.
Learn any new tool **only as needed**.
feel: Mostly **steady**, with a small knot about the matching software.
S0.quote: Nobody has said the payroll project is about cutting jobs, but nobody has said it isn't.
fieldNote: Her own job feels safe, but **routine screen work** around her is already being studied.
Her **resistance** is calm: she'd learn the minimum and nothing more.
She has a strong **habit of saving** from her father, which steadies her.

steps.text: Keep checking exceptions and signing off the monthly pay run
Pay extra off the flat's mortgage each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the change is real and the company should be honest about it. I'd ask for a clear plan on which roles change and when. I wouldn't campaign, but I'd want straight answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one gets close. Checking is on the card, and checking is all we do. If the software checks timesheets and works out overtime, my six people become two, and a team of two doesn't need a manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more aside, and I'd stop the extra mortgage payments so I've got cash on hand. I'd look quietly at payroll jobs in the council or the hospital, where things change slower. I'd hold off on any decision until the company actually announced something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel like I was waiting for a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they announced cuts, yes. There are lots of payroll jobs nearby, and I'm not proud. I'd rather move sideways to somewhere slower than be the last manager of a shrinking team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad would say keep your head down and your savings up. That's what he did when the steelworks cut half the office in the nineties. He kept his job by being the one who never made mistakes, and I'm the same kind of person.

say: I'd say the company should be **honest** about the change.
I'd ask for a **clear plan** on which roles change and when.
think: Checking is **all we do**, and checking is on the card.
If six people become two, a team of two **doesn't need a manager**.
do: Stop extra mortgage payments and **hold cash** instead.
Look quietly at **payroll jobs** at the council or hospital.
**Hold off** on deciding until the company announces something.
S1.quote: If the software checks timesheets and works out overtime, my six people become two, and a team of two doesn't need a manager.
fieldNote: She can see exactly how her **own role** disappears: through team shrinkage.
Her instinct is to **wait** for an announcement, then move sideways.
Her father's **steelworks story** shapes her idea of safety: never make mistakes.

steps.text: Stop extra mortgage payments and keep the money as cash
Browse payroll openings at the council and the hospital
Wait for the company's official announcement before acting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and somebody should slow it down. I'd want the government to say something sensible, like keeping people paid while they retrain. I'm not one for protests, but I'd vote on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd lose my job. Payroll is rules and numbers, the purest thinking work there is. And when the robots arrive around 2031, the drivers and warehouse staff go too, so there's nobody left to pay anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd cut my spending right back, no new car, no holiday. I'd look into a bookkeeping course for small businesses, because small firms might be slower to change. And I'd talk to my sister Ida about moving in with her if things got really bad, so I could rent out my flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's my whole working life in one sentence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the minimum. Would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would have to. I'd sit down with a tool for the first time, probably in the evenings, because being the one who's never used it would be the worst place to be. I'd hate it, but I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ida, first. She's a hairdresser, so she's hands-on, and she has a spare room. It would feel like going backwards, living with my big sister at nearly thirty, but she'd never let me sink.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and somebody should slow it down.
I'd want government to keep people **paid while they retrain**.
think: I'd **lose my job**, because payroll is pure rules and numbers.
When robots arrive around 2031, **drivers and warehouse staff** go too, leaving nobody to pay.
do: Cut spending right back: **no new car**, no holiday.
Look into a **bookkeeping course** for small businesses.
Ask my sister Ida about **moving in** and renting out my flat.
feel: **Alarmed**: it's my whole working life in one sentence.
S2.quote: When the robots arrive around 2031, the drivers and warehouse staff go too, so there's nobody left to pay anyway.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** outright and sees no corner of payroll that survives.
She links the **robot delay** to her own work: no workers, no payroll.
Her fallback is **family**: her sister's spare room, which feels like going backwards.

steps.text: Cut spending and skip the new car and holiday
Take an evening bookkeeping course for small businesses
Ask her sister Ida about moving in and letting the flat
Practise with an AI tool in the evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time, so let's be sensible about it. The company should tell people early and help them move. I'd say that at the staff forum, which is about as political as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think payroll goes later than other office jobs, because the law says someone has to be responsible for paying people correctly. But later still means before 2031. I'd have maybe four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job but apply for a payroll role at the hospital within two years. I'd keep saving and get the mortgage down as far as I could. I'd probably take a course in pension rules, because that's the fiddly area that stays human the longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less. More like knowing an exam is coming than being in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the hospital?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hospitals change slowly, and they've got thousands of nurses with complicated shifts. That's messy work. And if the worst happens, a public employer is more likely to look after its people than a parcel company chasing a share price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your company to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tell us the date, really. If I knew Payroll Simplification ended my team in 2030, I could plan. It's the not knowing that keeps me checking my emails at night.

say: I'd say we have time, so be **sensible** about it.
I'd ask the company at the **staff forum** to tell people early.
think: Payroll lasts a bit longer because someone must be **legally responsible**.
Later still means **before 2031**, so I'd have about four years.
do: Apply for a **hospital payroll** role within two years.
Keep saving and bring the **mortgage** down.
Take a course in **pension rules**, the fiddly part that stays human longest.
feel: **Anxious**, but less, like knowing an exam is coming.
S3.quote: Hospitals change slowly, and they've got thousands of nurses with complicated shifts.
fieldNote: She still expects to lose her current role, but she has a **plan with dates**.
She trusts **public employers** more than a firm chasing a share price.
Uncertainty about **timing** troubles her more than the change itself.

steps.text: Apply for a payroll role at the hospital within two years
Pay the mortgage down as far as possible
Take a course in pension rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people are honest about it. I'd tell the team not to panic. Online I'd say nothing, as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel fairly safe for most of the decade. I'd be 37 when it arrives, with the flat nearly paid off. The payroll job would still go at the end, but the end is a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and keep saving for the first few years. Around 2031 I'd move to the hospital or a council, somewhere public. Paying off the flat before 2036 is the one thing that would make me feel truly safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's on my mind, but it's not keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down, do the pay runs right, and pay off the flat. Maybe I'd learn some of the tools as they settled down, once everyone else had worked out the problems. I'm never first, but I'm never last either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk in waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the slow version is slower for the bosses than for us. Payroll Simplification might cut my team long before 2036. If that happened, I'd move sooner and use the savings to bridge any gap.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** if people are honest.
I'd tell the team **not to panic**.
think: I'd feel **fairly safe** for most of the decade.
The job **still goes** at the end, but the end is far off.
do: Keep my job and **keep saving** for the first few years.
feel: **Uneasy**: it's on my mind but not keeping me up.
S4.quote: Paying off the flat before 2036 is the one thing that would make me feel truly safe.
fieldNote: The long warning makes her feel her job is **safe for now**, so she's uneasy, not anxious.
Her plan rests on **paying off the flat**, her idea of real security.
She still sees the **payroll project** as a possible early cut.

steps.text: Keep running the payroll team for the next few years
Move to a council or hospital payroll role around 2031
Pay off the flat's mortgage before 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to move anywhere. What would help is a clear date. If the company told us when, and the government kept people paid while they retrained, I could cope with almost anything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that payroll is people's rent and food. When we get it wrong, someone can't pay their landlord. I'd want whatever replaces us to care about that as much as my team does.

headlineQuote: Payroll is people's rent and food. When we get it wrong, someone can't pay their landlord.
portrait: Nora is a 27-year-old **payroll manager** at a parcel delivery company, living alone in her own flat.
She has **ten months saved**, never uses AI tools and trusts the spreadsheets she built.
She is uneasy even in AI Plateau, because a **payroll project** is already studying her team's work.
In the fast AGI picture she expects to **lose her job** and would lean on her sister.
With more warning she'd move to a **public employer** and pay off her flat.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be **no time** to move anywhere.
whatWouldHelp: A **clear date** from the company and government pay while people **retrain**.
